Attention and felt closeness: a synthetic fixture study

Abstract
Sixty undergraduates held a short conversation with a confederate who either
attended to them or did not. Participants in the attention condition felt
closer to the confederate afterwards.

Methods
Sixty undergraduates took part in exchange for course credit, randomly assigned
in equal numbers to an attention or a control condition. Participants held a
short conversation with a confederate. In the attention condition the
confederate faced the participant, maintained eye contact and responded to what
the participant said. In the control condition the confederate looked at a form
on the desk and gave only minimal acknowledgements. Afterwards participants
rated how close they felt to the confederate on a single item from one (not at
all close) to seven (extremely close). We compared mean closeness between
conditions with a two-sided independent-samples t test assuming equal variances,
and computed Cohen's d with the pooled standard deviation. No participants were
excluded and there are no missing values.

Results
Closeness was higher in the attention condition (M = 4.09, SD = 0.66) than in
the control condition (M = 3.27, SD = 0.69), t(58) = 4.69, p < .001, d = 1.21.

Discussion
Being attended to during a brief conversation raised how close participants felt
to their partner.
